The Surah al-Ghashiyah is Meccan and has twenty-six verses.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Has the story of the Overwhelming (al-Ghashiyah) reached you?﴾ ﴿Faces that Day will be humbled,﴾ ﴿toiling and weary,﴾ ﴿burning in a scorching Fire,﴾ ﴿given to drink from a boiling spring,﴾ ﴿having no food except from ḍarī' (a thorny plant),﴾ ﴿which neither nourishes nor relieves hunger.﴾ ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant,﴾ [88:8] ﴿pleased with their striving,﴾ [88:9] ﴿in a lofty Garden,﴾ [88:10] ﴿where they will hear no idle talk,﴾ [88:11] ﴿therein a flowing spring,﴾ [88:12] ﴿therein raised couches,﴾ [88:13] ﴿and cups set out,﴾ [88:14] ﴿and cushions arranged in rows,﴾ [88:15] ﴿and carpets spread out.﴾ [88:16] ﴿Do they not look at the camels, how they were created?﴾ [88:17] ﴿And at the sky, how it was raised?﴾ [88:18] ﴿And at the mountains, how they were set firm?﴾ [88:19] ﴿And at the earth, how it was spread out?﴾ [88:20] ﴿So remind them; you are only a reminder.﴾ [88:21] ﴿You are not over them a controller,﴾ [88:22] ﴿except whoever turns away and disbelieves, then God will punish him with the greatest punishment.﴾ [88:23] ﴿Indeed, to Us is their return,﴾ [88:25] ﴿then indeed, upon Us is their reckoning.﴾ [88:26]

Ḍarī' (ḍarīʿ): Abu Hanifa said, and I think he meant the authority on plants, that ḍarī' is al-shibriq (a wild plant), which is poor pasture; livestock that graze on it gain neither fat nor flesh. From this is the verse of Ibn ʿAzzarah al-Hudhali:

"And they were confined in the hollow of ḍarī', so all of them are hunched, with bleeding hands, and shy of being mounted."

Abu Dhu'ayb said:

"It grazed on the green shibriq until it withered, and became ḍarī', and the scrapings fell away from it."

Some linguists said: it is the dried stalks of ʿarfaj (a plant) when it crumbles. Al-Zajjaj said: it is a plant like the ʿawsaj (a thorny shrub). Al-Khalil said: it is a green plant with a foul smell, which the sea throws up. Al-Namariq (cushions) are the pillows; their singular is numruqah, with the nun and the ra' both pronounced with a damma or both with a kasra.

Zuhayr said:

"Elders and youths, handsome of face, upon couches arranged in rows and cushions."

Al-Zarabi (carpets) are broad, splendid rugs. Al-Farra' said: they are embroidered cushions; the singular is zirbiyyah, with the zay either kasra or fatha. Sutihat al-ard (the earth was spread out) means it was spread and trodden upon.

This surah is Meccan. Since the preceding verses mention "so remind" and mention the Fire and the Hereafter, God says: ﴿Has the story of the Overwhelming reached you?﴾ Al-Ghashiyah is the calamity that overwhelms people with its hardships on the Day of Resurrection; this is the view of Sufyan and the majority. This interrogative is a notice of attention, and its purpose is to stir the listener's soul to receive the report. It was said: the meaning is, "Did this knowledge come to you except that We taught you?" In this there is an enumeration of the blessing. It was also said: hal (هل) here means qad (قد). ﴿Faces that Day﴾: that is, on the day when it was overwhelmed. The tanwin (تنوين) is a 'iwad (substitute) for a clause, and no clause preceded that could be substituted by the tanwin; but since the word al-ghashiyah has preceded, and the definite article al (ال) is a relative (موصولة) joined to the active participle, it is resolved as "the one which overwhelmed," that is, "the calamity which overwhelmed." So the tanwin is a substitute for this clause into which the word al-ghashiyah is resolved, and for the relative noun which is "the one which" (التي). ﴿Humbled﴾: abased.

It was said: its work in the Fire is dragging chains and shackles, its wading in the Fire like camels wading in mud, and its climbing up a mountain of fire and descending its slopes, constantly. Ibn ʿAbbas also said, along with Zayd ibn Aslam and Ibn Jubayr: toiling in this world and weary in it, because they were not upon guidance; so there is no fruit for them except weariness, and its end is the Fire. The verse refers to monks, worshippers of idols, and every person striving in his disbelief. ʿIkrimah and al-Suddi said: (ʿāmilatan nāṣibatan) in the accusative, as a expression of blame; the majority read them in the nominative.

And [Ibn Muhaysin] recited tuṣlā (تَصْلَى) with a fatha on the ta'; Abu Raja' and Ibn Muhaysin and the two Abus (Abu ʿAmr and Abu Bakr) with a damma; and Kharijah with a damma on the ta' and a fatha on the ṣad, with the lam doubled; Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla' has transmitted this reading.

ḥāmiyah (scorching): kindled. Āniyah (boiling): its heat has reached its limit, like His saying: ﴿between it and boiling water﴾ [55:44]; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan and Mujahid. Ibn Zayd said: it is present for them, from the saying "ānā al-shay'" (the thing was present). As for ḍarī': Ibn ʿAbbas said: a tree of fire. Al-Husayn and a group said: al-zaqqum (a bitter tree). Ibn Jubayr said: stones of fire. Ibn ʿAbbas also said, and Qatadah, ʿIkrimah and Mujahid: the shibriq of the Fire. It was said: al-ʿabashraq. It was said: moist ʿarfaj; what was said about it has been mentioned in the vocabulary section. It was also said: a valley in Hell.

If ḍarī' is al-ghislin and al-zaqqum, then it is clear, and the restriction in ﴿except from ghislin﴾ [69:36] and ﴿except from ḍarī'﴾ is not contradictory. If they are different things, the reconciliation is that al-zaqqum is for one group, al-ghislin for another group, and ḍarī' for another group.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿neither nourishes﴾ is in a place of nominative or genitive, as a description of ṭaʿām (food) or ḍarī'. He means that their food is something that is not among the foods of humans; it is thorn, and thorn is among what camels graze on and are fond of, and this is a type of it from which they shy away and do not approach; and the two benefits of nourishment are absent from it: removing hunger and providing strength, and fattening the body. End quote.

His saying "in a place of nominative or genitive, as a description of ṭaʿām or ḍarī'" — as for its being genitive as a description of ḍarī', this is correct, because it is affirmed, and fattening and relieving hunger are negated from it. As for its being nominative as a description of ṭaʿām, this is not correct, because ṭaʿām is negated, and "does not fatten" is negated too, so its composition is not sound. The sense becomes: "They have no food which does not fatten nor relieve hunger except from ḍarī'," so the meaning becomes: they have food that fattens and relieves hunger apart from ḍarī'; just as you say: "Zayd has no property that he does not benefit from except from the property of ʿAmr," meaning he has property from which he benefits apart from ʿAmr's property. If it were said that the clause is in the place of a nominative description for the omitted noun in "except from ḍarī'," it would be correct, since it is in the place of a nominative as a substitute for the subject of laysa (ليس), meaning "they have no food except that which is from ḍarī'," for feeding from ḍarī' neither fattens nor relieves hunger; this is a sound composition and a clear meaning.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: or it is intended that they have no food at all, because ḍarī' is not food even for beasts, let alone for humans, since food is that which satisfies and fattens, and it is far from both. Just as you say: "So-and-so has no shade except the sun," meaning the negation of shade by emphasis. End quote.

On this view, the exception is disjunctive (munqaṭiʿ), since what comes from ḍarī' is not included under the word ṭaʿām, as it is not food. The apparent reading is that the exception is connected (muttaṣil). The same holds for His saying: ﴿nor food except from ghislin﴾ [69:36], because ṭaʿām is what a person eats, and this is a common notion between what is pleasant, what is disliked, and what is neither pleasant nor disliked.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 88, verses 8–26:**

﴿Faces that day will be joyful﴾. The indefinite noun (*nakira*) is permissible as the subject of a nominal sentence here, and also in his words ﴿Faces that day will be humbled﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 2], because there is a justification for it, which is that it is detailed (*tafsil*). *Nā'imah* means beautiful and radiant, or *mutan'immah* (enjoying bliss).

﴿Pleased with their striving﴾, that is, for their deeds in the world through obedience, pleased when that deed's reward is Paradise. ﴿In a lofty garden﴾, that is, lofty in place and in rank. Al-A'raj, the people of Makkah and Madinah, Nafi', Ibn Kathir, and Abu 'Amr, according to one of the transmissions from them, read (*lā tusma'*) in the passive voice, and (*lāghiyah*) is in the nominative case, meaning "a vain word" or "a vain assembly," or "vain talk" (*laghw*), in which case it is a verbal noun like *al-'āqibah*. There are three opinions on this. The third is the reading of Abu 'Ubaydah, Ibn Muhaysin, 'Isa, and Ibn Kathir, and Abu 'Amr likewise, except that they read it with *yā'* (*yusma'*) because the feminine is metaphorical. Al-Fadl and al-Jahdari likewise, except that he put *lāghiyah* in the accusative, in the sense of "no one hears in it," from your saying "I made Zayd hear" (*asma'tu Zaydan*). Al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Abu Ja'far, Qatadah, Ibn Sirin, Nafi' in the transmission of Kharijah, and Abu 'Amr according to one transmission from him, and the rest of the seven, read *lā tasma'*, with the *tā'* of address, generally, or addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ), or the subject is the one who exists. (*lāghiyatan*) in the accusative. ﴿In it is a flowing spring﴾. *'Ayn* is a noun of genus, meaning springs, or it is a specific spring mentioned to honour it. ﴿In it are raised couches﴾, raised in rank or raised in place, so that he sees what his Lord has bestowed upon him of dominion and bliss; or *marfū'ah* means concealed (*makhbū'ah*), from *rafa'tu laka hadha*, meaning I hid it.

﴿And cups set in place﴾, that is, prepared with their drinks, not needing one to fill them; or set before them; or set on the edges of the springs. ﴿And cushions arranged in rows﴾, that is, cushions arranged side by side for leaning upon and reclining against. ﴿And carpets spread out﴾, scattered here and there in the assemblies.

When the Exalted mentioned the matter of the Resurrection and the division of its people into wretched and blessed, and it was known that there is no way to establish this except through the Wise Creator, He followed this with mention of these signs, and of what the Arabs constantly witness and deal with, so He said: ﴿Do they not look at the camels, how they were created?﴾. The camel is meant here, for in it are gathered the benefits that are scattered among other things: eating its meat, drinking its milk, carrying loads upon it, traveling upon it to distant lands, its ability to live on whatever plant it eats, its patience with thirst, to the extent that some of them can go ten days without water, its docility toward whoever leads it, its ability to rise while kneeling under heavy loads, its large number of offspring, and its responsiveness to a beautiful voice despite the hardness of its liver. No other animal combines these qualities. The Exalted has made clear His favour to them (p-464) in His words: ﴿Do they not see that We have created for them, of what Our hands have made, cattle?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 71] and so on. Because it was the best thing among the Arabs, they made it the blood-money for killing, and they gave a hundred of them to whoever came to them or whom they wished to honour. The poets mentioned them in praise of one who gave them, as one said:

"They gave Hunayda, eight driving her [camels]..."

Another said:

"The giver of a hundred noble camels with their whole herd..."

The mention of the clouds alongside the camel fits with directing attention to the camel and to the wondrous attributes it contains, along with what is mentioned with it: the sky, the mountains, and the earth, because these things are arranged together in the eyes of the Arabs in their valleys and their deserts, and to indicate reasoning toward establishing the Creator, and that He is not restricted to one kind rather than another, but is general in all His creations, as it is said:

"In everything there is a sign pointing that He is One."

Abu al-'Abbas al-Mubarrad said: the camel here means the cloud, because the Arabs sometimes call it by that name, since it comes in files like camels, is driven as camels are driven, and sometimes in its shape resembles camels and ostriches. From this is his saying:

"As if the clouds between the sky... are ostriches suspended by their tethers..."

Al-Zamakhshari said: whoever claims that "the camel" means the cloud does so only out of seeking a fitting connection, and perhaps he did not mean that *al-ibil* is one of the names of cloud, like *al-ghamam*, *al-muzn*, *al-rabab*, and *al-ghaym*, and so on, but rather he saw the cloud frequently compared to camels in their poetry, so he permitted that it be meant by it, by way of comparison and metaphor. End of quote.

The majority read (*al-ibili*) with a *kasrah* on the *bā'* and a light *lām*. Al-Asma'i, from Abu 'Amr, read it with a *sukūn* on the *bā'*. 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas read it with a shadda on the *lām*. It is also transmitted from Abu 'Amr, Abu Ja'far, and al-Kisa'i, and they said it means the cloud, according to some people of the language. Al-Hasan said: He singled out the camel for mention because it eats date-pits and fodder and produces milk. It was said to him: the elephant is greater in wonder. He said: the Arabs are far removed from knowledge of the elephant. Moreover it is a pig whose meat is not eaten, whose back is not ridden, and whose milk is not milked. The word *ibil* has no singular from its own form, and it is feminine; therefore when diminutized the *tā'* is added, so they say *ubaylah*, and in the plural they say *'ābāl*. They have derived from its form, so they say *ta'abbala al-rajul* (the man became a camel-herd), and they marveled at this verb irregularly, so they say *mā ābala Zaydan* (how much Zayd is a camel-herd!). *Ibl* is a noun that came in the pattern *fi'l*, and Sibawayh did not record any other word of this pattern.

﴿How it was created﴾ is an interrogative clause in the position of an apposition (*badal*) to *al-ibil*. *Yanzurūna* transitively reaches *al-ibil* through *ilā*, and *ilā kayfa khuliqat* is in the mode of suspension (*ta'līq*). A clause containing an interrogative may be substituted for the noun preceding it, as in the saying "I knew Zayd, who is his father?" according to the most correct opinions, since the Arabs have introduced *ilā* before *kayfa*. It is related that they said: "Look at how he does it" (*unẓur ilā kayfa yaṣna'u*). *Kayfa* is a question about a state, and its governing element is *khuliqat*. When the verb is suspended from what contains the interrogative, the interrogative no longer remains in its literal sense. We have explained this in our book called *al-Tadhkirah* and elsewhere.

The majority read (*khuliqat, rufi'at, nusibat*) and (*suṭiḥat*) with the feminine *tā'* and in the passive voice. 'Ali, Abu Haywah, and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read them with the *tā'* of the speaker in the active voice, the object being omitted, meaning: I created it, I raised it, I set it up. (*rufi'at*) raised, a height at a great distance without pillars. (*nusibat*) set firmly, not leaning and not moving. (*suṭiḥat*) spread out, until it became like a bed for one who lies down upon it. The majority read (*suṭiḥat*) with a light *ṭā'*, while al-Hasan and Harun read it with a shadda. When He urged them to reflection, He commanded His Messenger to remind them, so He said: ﴿So remind﴾ (*fa dhakkir*). Let not their failure to look trouble you. ﴿You are only a reminder﴾, like His words: ﴿Upon you is only the delivering [of the message]﴾ [al-Shura: 48], ﴿You are not over them a controller﴾, that is, not a dominator, like His words: ﴿And you are not over them a compeller﴾ [Qaf: 45]. The majority read (*musayṭir*) with *ṣād* and a *kasrah* on the *ṭā'*. Ibn 'Amir in one transmission, Nutayq from Qunbul, and Zar'an from Hafs read it with *sīn*. Hamzah in one transmission read it with the sign of *ishmām* for the *zāy* (a faint *z*-sound). Harun read it with a *fatḥah* on the *ṭā'*, which is the dialect of Tamim. *Sayṭara* is transitive according to them, and the reflexive verb *tasayṭara* points to this. In the language, in this pattern (*fu'ayil*-type), there are only *musayṭir*, *muhayman*, *mubayṭir*, and *mubayqir*, which are active participles from *sayṭara*, *haymana*, and *bayṭara*. *Mujayjir* came as the name of a valley, and *mudayabir*. It is possible that the original forms of these two were *mudabbir* and *mujammir*, and they were diminutized.

The majority read (*illā*) as an exceptive particle. It was said that it is connected, meaning: "so you are a controller over him." It was also said: it is connected to (*fa dhakkir*), meaning: "so remind, except him who has been cut off from hope in his faith and turned away, so he deserves the greatest punishment," and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection. It was also said that it is disconnected, and this is a verse of acceptance (*muwada'ah*), abrogated by the verse of the sword. Ibn 'Abbas, Zayd ibn 'Ali, Qatadah, and Zayd ibn Aslam read (*alā*) as an interjection of attention and beginning. The greatest punishment is the punishment of Hell.

The majority read (*iyābahum*) with a light *yā'*, the verbal noun of *āba*. Abu Ja'far and Shaybah read it with a shadda, as a verbal noun of *fa'yala* from *ayyaba*, on the pattern *fi'āl*, or a verbal noun of *fa'wala* like *ḥawqala*, on the pattern *fi'āl* also like *ḥiqāl*, or a verbal noun of *fa'ūl* like *jahūr*, on the pattern *fa'wāl* like *jahwār*. Its origin is *awwāb*, so the first *wāw* was changed to *yā'* because it was quiescent and the letter before it was kasrah-ed. In this pattern, and the two patterns before it, there is a *wāw* and a *yā'*, and one of them preceded with a *sukūn*, so the *wāw* was changed to *yā'* and assimilated. The assimilation did not prevent the change, because the *wāw* and the *yā'* are not the root letters of the verb; rather the *yā'* in *fa'yala* and the *wāw* in *fa'ūl* are additional letters. Ṣāḥib al-Lawāmiḥ said, and al-Zamakhshari followed him: its origin is *iwwāban*, the verbal noun of *awwaba*, like *kadhdhaba kidhdhāban*. Then it became *iywāban*, so the first *wāw* was changed to *yā'* because the letter before it was kasrah-ed. Al-Zamakhshari said: like *diywān* in *dīwān*. Then what was done to it was done to *sayyid*; he means that a *yā'* and a *wāw* came together, and one of them preceded with a *sukūn*, so the *wāw* was changed to *yā'* and the *yā'* was assimilated into the *wāw*. As for it being a verbal noun of *awwaba*, this is not permissible, because they stated that when the first *wāw* is established for assimilation and the letter before it is kasrah-ed, the first *wāw* is not changed to *yā'* on account of the kasrah. They gave as examples *ikhrīwāṭ*, the verbal noun of *ikhrawwaṭa*, and also the verbal noun of *awwaba*, like *awwaba iwwābān*. These were established on assimilation, so it protected them from substitution and they were not affected by the kasrah. As for al-Zamakhshari's comparison with *dīwān*, it is not a good one, because they did not pronounce it assimilated in the original form, so they did not say *dawwān*. Were it not for the plural *dawāwīn*, it would not be known that the origin of this *yā'* is a *wāw*. Also, they stated that *dīwān* is an anomaly, so nothing else may be analogized to it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it may also be from *a'wab*, so it comes as *iywāb*, the hamza being eased; and the requirement in assimilation would be to return it as *iwwāb*, but the *yā'* was preferred in it against analogy. End of quote. His saying "the requirement in assimilation would be to return it as *iwwāb*" is not correct; rather, the requirement, when assimilation is considered, is that it be *iyyāb*, because a *yā'*, which is the letter substituted for the hamza by easing, came together with a *wāw* which is the root letter of the word, and one of them is quiescent, so the *wāw* is changed to *yā'* and the *yā'* is assimilated into it, so it becomes *iyyāb*.

Since it is among al-Zamakhshari's principles that the preposing of the object (*ma'mūl*) gives restriction, he said its meaning is: their return is only to the Almighty, the Powerful over vengeance, and their reckoning is incumbent only upon Him, the Exalted, who reckons the smallest speck and the thinnest membrane. The meaning of "incumbent" is incumbency in wisdom. And Allah knows best.

﴿Pleased with their striving﴾, that is, for their deeds in the world through obedience, pleased when that deed's reward is Paradise. ﴿In a lofty garden﴾, that is, lofty in place and in rank. Al-A'raj, the people of Makkah and Madinah, Nafi', Ibn Kathir, and Abu 'Amr, according to one of the transmissions from them, read (*lā tusma'*) in the passive voice, and (*lāghiyah*) is in the nominative case, meaning "a vain word" or "a vain assembly," or "vain talk" (*laghw*), in which case it is a verbal noun like *al-'āqibah*. There are three opinions on this. The third is the reading of Abu 'Ubaydah, Ibn Muhaysin, 'Isa, and Ibn Kathir, and Abu 'Amr likewise, except that they read it with *yā'* (*yusma'*) because the feminine is metaphorical. Al-Fadl and al-Jahdari likewise, except that he put *lāghiyah* in the accusative, in the sense of "no one hears in it," from your saying "I made Zayd hear" (*asma'tu Zaydan*). Al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Abu Ja'far, Qatadah, Ibn Sirin, Nafi' in the transmission of Kharijah, and Abu 'Amr according to one transmission from him, and the rest of the seven, read *lā tasma'*, with the *tā'* of address, generally, or addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ), or the subject is the one who exists. (*lāghiyatan*) in the accusative. ﴿In it is a flowing spring﴾. *'Ayn* is a noun of genus, meaning springs, or it is a specific spring mentioned to honour it. ﴿In it are raised couches﴾, raised in rank or raised in place, so that he sees what his Lord has bestowed upon him of dominion and bliss; or *marfū'ah* means concealed (*makhbū'ah*), from *rafa'tu laka hadha*, meaning I hid it.

﴿And cups set in place﴾, that is, prepared with their drinks, not needing one to fill them; or set before them; or set on the edges of the springs. ﴿And cushions arranged in rows﴾, that is, cushions arranged side by side for leaning upon and reclining against. ﴿And carpets spread out﴾, scattered here and there in the assemblies.

When the Exalted mentioned the matter of the Resurrection and the division of its people into wretched and blessed, and it was known that there is no way to establish this except through the Wise Creator, He followed this with mention of these signs, and of what the Arabs constantly witness and deal with, so He said: ﴿Do they not look at the camels, how they were created?﴾. The camel is meant here, for in it are gathered the benefits that are scattered among other things: eating its meat, drinking its milk, carrying loads upon it, traveling upon it to distant lands, its ability to live on whatever plant it eats, its patience with thirst, to the extent that some of them can go ten days without water, its docility toward whoever leads it, its ability to rise while kneeling under heavy loads, its large number of offspring, and its responsiveness to a beautiful voice despite the hardness of its liver. No other animal combines these qualities. The Exalted has made clear His favour to them (p-464) in His words: ﴿Do they not see that We have created for them, of what Our hands have made, cattle?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 71] and so on. Because it was the best thing among the Arabs, they made it the blood-money for killing, and they gave a hundred of them to whoever came to them or whom they wished to honour. The poets mentioned them in praise of one who gave them, as one said:

"They gave Hunayda, eight driving her [camels]..."

Another said:

"The giver of a hundred noble camels with their whole herd..."

"In everything there is a sign pointing that He is One."
